site.name: UniPath Africa
site.tagline: Your journey to university, made simpler.
site.heroTitle: Find a university that fits your future.
site.heroSubtitle: One guided path from discovering programs to enrolling — built for African students applying at home and abroad. Match by your grades, budget and goals, prepare every document, and never miss a deadline.
site.announcementText: We're testing UniPath Africa with students — try it and tell us what you think.
site.dataNotice: Each programme is labelled: “Verified” (fees checked on the official website), “On official list” (programme confirmed by the university, fees estimated) or “Indicative” (estimates). Always confirm fees and deadlines on the university’s official website before paying anything.
site.plansNote: Pilot prices — we’re testing what is fair and affordable. Core guidance will always stay free, and we never charge for admission guarantees (there is no such thing).
site.scopeNote: UniPath Africa is a guidance platform. We are not a visa agent, we don’t submit visa applications, and no one can guarantee admission. Universities make all admission decisions, and visas are handled directly with official embassies and immigration offices.
site.consultationHours: Monday–Saturday, 9am–6pm (East Africa Time) · WhatsApp, phone or Google Meet
site.freeNote: No fees, no hidden charges. Every tool and every adviser session on UniPath is free until further notice.

checklistItems.label: Complete the online application form
checklistItems.tip: Use exactly the same name spelling as on your passport or national ID.

checklistItems.label: Academic transcripts / results slips
checklistItems.tip: Request certified copies early — schools can take 1–3 weeks.

checklistItems.label: Certificates (e.g. UCE/UACE, KCSE, WASSCE)
checklistItems.tip: If results are pending, most universities accept provisional results first.

checklistItems.label: National ID or passport copy
checklistItems.tip: Scan in colour, all four corners visible.

checklistItems.label: Personal statement / motivation letter
checklistItems.tip: Write it in the Statement Studio — it checks length and clichés for you.

checklistItems.label: Pay the application fee (official channel only)
checklistItems.tip: Pay only through the university's official portal or bank account. Keep the receipt.

checklistItems.label: Birth certificate
checklistItems.tip: Some public universities ask for it at registration.

checklistItems.label: Check government sponsorship / loan eligibility
checklistItems.tip: Compare merit, district quota and student-loan options before paying privately.

checklistItems.label: Valid passport
checklistItems.tip: Ideally valid for your whole planned stay. Renewals can take weeks.

checklistItems.label: English test results (IELTS/TOEFL/Duolingo) or waiver
checklistItems.tip: Many universities waive tests for English-medium schooling — ask for a waiver letter.

checklistItems.label: Recommendation letters
checklistItems.tip: Ask referees at least 4–6 weeks before the deadline. Use the Reference Kit.

checklistItems.label: Proof of funds / bank statement
checklistItems.tip: Usually needed for the visa; check the exact amount and how recent it must be.

checklistItems.label: Check qualification equivalency
checklistItems.tip: Confirm whether your certificate needs a foundation year or credential evaluation.

checklistItems.label: Research visa / study permit requirements
checklistItems.tip: Look up the official immigration website for your destination country.

checklistItems.label: Academic CV
checklistItems.tip: Two pages max. Lead with education, research and relevant work.

checklistItems.label: Degree certificate and transcript
checklistItems.tip: If you haven't graduated yet, a provisional transcript is usually fine.

glossary.definition: An offer of admission that becomes final only after you meet stated conditions, such as final exam results or an English test score.
An offer with no academic conditions left to meet. You may still need to accept, pay a deposit, or register by a deadline.
A short essay explaining why you want to study the course, what prepared you, and what you hope to do next.
The postgraduate version of a personal statement — more focused on academic interests, research and career plans.
An official record of the subjects you took and the grades you earned, issued by your school or university.
In Uganda's UACE, a pass at A-level standard (grades A–E) in a principal subject. Universities usually ask for at least two.
How your certificate compares to the entry requirements of another country's system. Some countries require a foundation year.
A one-year preparatory programme that bridges your secondary qualification to a degree in another education system.
A payment some universities request to hold your place. Pay only through official university channels.
Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies — a reference number a UK university gives you to apply for a Student visa.
A US form issued by your university that you need to apply for an F-1 student visa.
Permission to study in a country such as Canada. Usually requires an acceptance letter and proof of funds.
A bank account (common for Germany) holding a fixed amount you can withdraw monthly — used as proof of funds for a visa.
Applications are reviewed as they arrive until places fill, so applying early improves your chances.
Permission to apply without paying the application fee — often available for students with financial need. Always ask.
The month a programme starts (e.g. August or January). Some universities have more than one intake per year.
A US fee (I-901) every F-1 student pays before the visa interview.
Confirmation of Enrolment — the document an Australian university issues so you can apply for a student visa.
Provincial (or territorial) attestation letter. Most new students need one to apply for a Canadian study permit.
A UK fee paid with your visa that gives you access to the NHS. £776 per year for students.
Your fingerprints and photo, taken at a visa centre as part of most visa applications.
Bank statements, sponsor letters or scholarship letters showing you can pay tuition and living costs.
A signed letter from the person paying for your studies saying how much they will pay and how they are related to you.
Emergency money a university gives students who suddenly can’t pay for essentials. Ask the financial aid or student affairs office.
Times each week when lecturers wait in their office for students to drop in with questions. Free and under-used.
How much a course counts towards your degree. Courses with more credits affect your average more.
Cumulative grade point average — your average across all your courses so far.
A plan for where your money will go before you spend it.
Savings kept only for real emergencies, like illness or a broken laptop.
The price of borrowing money, or what a bank pays you for saving.
Annual percentage rate — the yearly cost of a loan including interest and most fees. Use it to compare loans.
The amount of money you borrowed, before interest.
Interest earned (or charged) on earlier interest as well as the original amount.
How much of one currency you get for another. It changes every day.
Savings and credit cooperative — members save together and can borrow at fair rates.
Your full salary before tax and other deductions.
Your take-home pay after tax and deductions.
Pay As You Earn — income tax your employer deducts from your salary.
An organisation that records how people repay loans. Lenders check it before lending.

faqs.a: Yes. Discovering programmes, matching, checklists, the document vault, the tracker and all preparation tools are free. In future we may offer optional paid human support — core guidance will stay free.

faqs.q: Does a match mean I will be admitted?
faqs.a: No. A match shows programmes that appear to fit your results, budget and goals based on published requirements. Universities make all admission decisions.

When you create a free account, your profile, applications and documents are stored securely on UniPath’s servers so you can use any device and our advisers can help you. Without an account, everything stays only on the device you’re using. You can download or delete your data at any time.

faqs.q: Can I apply directly through UniPath?
faqs.a: Not yet. We link you to each university's official application portal and help you prepare and track everything. Direct submission will come with university partnerships.

faqs.q: Do universities pay to appear higher?
faqs.a: No. Matches are ranked only by how well a programme fits you. Any future partnership will be clearly disclosed.

faqs.q: How accurate are fees and deadlines?
faqs.a: Figures marked 'Indicative' are estimates. Programmes marked 'Verified' have been checked against the official website on the date shown. Always confirm on the official site before paying anything.

faqs.q: I don't have my final results yet. Can I still use it?
faqs.a: Yes. Use your predicted or mock results. Many universities accept applications before final results and make a conditional offer.

faqs.q: Can I use it on my phone with poor internet?
faqs.a: Yes. UniPath works on any phone browser and keeps working offline once loaded. You can also add it to your home screen like an app.

faqs.q: Do you process visas or guarantee admission?
faqs.a: No. We guide you and help you prepare, but universities make every admission decision and visas are handled directly with official embassies and immigration offices. Be careful of anyone who promises guaranteed admission or a visa for a fee.

faqs.q: How do I talk to a real person?
faqs.a: Tap ‘Talk to an adviser’ at the top of any page to book a free consultation by WhatsApp, phone or Google Meet.

faqs.q: Does UniPath apply for my visa?
faqs.a: No. You apply yourself on the official government website, which is cheaper and safer. We help you prepare: the documents checklist, how much money to show, a timeline, interview practice and a free document check with an adviser. Open any country’s “Visa help” tab.

enrollSteps.title: Understand your offer
enrollSteps.detail: Is it conditional or unconditional? Note every condition, the acceptance deadline and any deposit required.

enrollSteps.title: Compare offers and costs
enrollSteps.detail: Use the Cost Planner to compare the full cost of each offer, including living costs and scholarships.

enrollSteps.title: Accept your chosen offer
enrollSteps.detail: Accept through the official portal before the deadline. Politely decline the others so places go to other students.

enrollSteps.title: Pay deposit or fees — safely
enrollSteps.detail: Use only the bank details printed on the official offer letter or portal. Never pay an agent's personal account.

enrollSteps.title: Confirm funding
enrollSteps.detail: Get written confirmation of any scholarship, sponsorship or loan, and know when funds are released.

enrollSteps.title: Arrange accommodation
enrollSteps.detail: Apply for university housing early, or research verified private hostels close to campus.

enrollSteps.title: Visa or study permit (if studying abroad)
enrollSteps.detail: Gather your CAS/I-20/acceptance letter, proof of funds and passport, then apply on the official government website.

enrollSteps.title: Health checks and insurance
enrollSteps.detail: Complete any medical forms, vaccinations and health insurance the university or visa requires.

enrollSteps.title: Plan travel and arrival
enrollSteps.detail: Book travel after your visa is approved. Note orientation dates and airport pick-up options.

enrollSteps.title: Register and attend orientation
enrollSteps.detail: Bring original documents for verification, complete registration, and get your student ID.

visaInterview.q: Why did you choose this course?
visaInterview.tip: Link it to what you studied before and the job you want. Be specific — name a module or skill.

visaInterview.q: Why this university and not one at home?
visaInterview.tip: Mention 1–2 real reasons: a module, ranking in your field, a scholarship, practical training. Avoid “it was easy to get in”.

visaInterview.q: Who is paying for your studies?
visaInterview.tip: Name the person or scholarship, their job or source of income, and the exact amount. It must match your documents.

visaInterview.q: What will you do after you graduate?
visaInterview.tip: Give a clear plan that brings you back home or builds your career — a role, an employer type, or a business idea.

visaInterview.q: What do your parents (or sponsor) do?
visaInterview.tip: Answer simply and confidently. Know their income roughly and how long they have done this work.

visaInterview.q: Have you been refused a visa before?
visaInterview.tip: Always tell the truth. Hiding a refusal is far worse than the refusal itself.

visaInterview.q: How much is your tuition and how much will you spend on living costs?
visaInterview.tip: Know both numbers from your offer / I-20 / CAS by heart.

visaInterview.q: Why do you want to study in the United States?
visaInterview.tip: Be specific about the programme and university; show you have researched it.

visaInterview.q: Do you have relatives in the United States?
visaInterview.tip: Answer honestly. Having relatives is not a problem; hiding them is.

visaInterview.q: What ties do you have to your home country?
visaInterview.tip: Family, property, a job offer, a family business, plans that need you at home.

visaInterview.q: Where will you live and how far is it from campus?
visaInterview.tip: Know your planned accommodation and the city.

visaInterview.q: Tell me about one module on your course.
visaInterview.tip: Pick one you are genuinely interested in and say why it helps your goals.

visaInterview.q: How does this course connect to your previous studies?
visaInterview.tip: Show a logical step forward — not a random change of field. If it is a change, explain why.

scamWarnings: No one can guarantee you a visa or an admission. Anyone who promises this is lying.
Never pay visa fees to a person — pay only on the official government website or at the official visa centre.
Fake admission letters and fake bank statements are common. Using them can get you banned for years.
Check that any “agent” is listed by the university itself on its official website.
Embassies and universities do not ask you to pay via mobile money to a personal number.
“Job + visa” packages abroad are usually scams or trafficking — be very careful.

moneyLessons.title: Make a budget that actually works
moneyLessons.summary: A budget is a plan for your money before you spend it — not a punishment.
body: A budget simply answers one question: “Where will my money go this month?” You write down the money coming in, then decide where every shilling goes before you spend it.
Start with needs (rent, food, transport, fees, data for classes), then savings (pay yourself next, even a little), and only then wants (going out, new clothes, extras).

A simple starting split for students is about 70% needs, 10% savings and 20% wants. If your needs are more than 100% of your income, you don’t have a budgeting problem — you have an income or cost problem, and it’s time to talk to family, the financial aid office or an adviser.
Check your budget every month against what you really spent. Most people underestimate food, transport and “small things” by a lot. Your phone’s mobile money statement is a free spending diary.
keyPoints: Needs first, then savings, then wants
Compare plan vs real spending every month
Small daily spends add up fast
quiz: What should you pay first when money arrives? | Going out with friends ; Needs like rent and fees, then savings ; Whatever comes up first | 2 | Needs keep you housed and studying; saving next protects you from surprises.
You earn UGX 400,000 a month. Roughly how much is 10% savings? | UGX 4,000 ; UGX 40,000 ; UGX 400,000 | 2 | 10% of 400,000 is 40,000.

Your budget says food is UGX 150,000 but you spent 230,000. What should you do? | Ignore it ; Adjust next month’s plan and cut something else ; Borrow to cover it every month | 2 | A budget is a living plan — adjust it to reality and rebalance.

moneyLessons.title: Saving and your emergency fund
moneyLessons.summary: Saving isn’t about being rich. It’s about not panicking when something goes wrong.
body: An emergency fund is money you keep only for real emergencies: illness, a broken laptop, a family crisis. A good first target for a student is one month of living costs.
Pay yourself first: move savings out the day money arrives — before you can spend it. Even UGX 10,000 a week is UGX 520,000 a year.
Keep savings separate from spending money: a different mobile money wallet, a savings account, or a trusted SACCO. If you can see it every day, you will spend it.
Interest is what a bank pays you for keeping money with it. With compound interest you earn interest on your interest, so starting early matters more than saving big.
keyPoints: Emergency fund = 1 month of costs to start
Save on payday, not at month end
quiz: What is an emergency fund for? | A new phone ; Real surprises like illness or a broken laptop ; Weekend trips | 2 | Only real emergencies — otherwise it won’t be there when you need it.
Saving UGX 10,000 every week for a year gives about… | UGX 120,000 ; UGX 520,000 ; UGX 1,000,000 | 2 | 52 weeks × 10,000 = 520,000.
Why keep savings in a separate place? | It earns more ; You’re less likely to spend it ; Banks require it | 2 | Out of sight, out of mind — separation protects your savings.

moneyLessons.title: Banks, mobile money and SACCOs
moneyLessons.summary: Where you keep your money changes how safe it is and how much it costs you.
body: Mobile money is fast and everywhere, but sending and withdrawing usually costs a fee. Many small withdrawals cost more than one planned withdrawal.
Bank accounts are safer for larger amounts, give you statements (needed for visas and loans) and often have student accounts with low fees. Ask for the full list of charges before opening one.
SACCOs (savings and credit cooperatives) let members save together and borrow at fair rates. Only join registered SACCOs with a good reputation.
Protect your PIN like your passport. No real bank, mobile money agent, university or scholarship will ever ask for your PIN.
keyPoints: Know the fees before you transact
Use a bank account for bigger sums and statements
quiz: Why might you need a bank statement? | For a visa or loan application ; To get a student ID ; To register for classes | 1 | Embassies and lenders ask for statements as proof of money.
Which saves fees? | Many small withdrawals ; One planned withdrawal ; Sending to yourself | 2 | Fewer transactions usually means fewer fees.
Someone from “the bank” asks for your PIN to fix your account. You… | Share it quickly ; Refuse and call the bank’s official number ; Send half the PIN | 2 | Real banks never ask for your PIN.

moneyLessons.title: Interest, loans and student loans
moneyLessons.summary: A loan is future-you paying for today. Know exactly how much it costs before you sign.
body: When you borrow, you pay back the amount you borrowed (the principal) plus interest — the price of borrowing.
Always ask for the yearly cost (APR) and the total amount you will repay. A loan that “only” costs 5% a month costs about 80% a year once it compounds.

Government student loans — like the Higher Education Students’ Financing Board (HESFB) in Uganda, HELB in Kenya and HESLB in Tanzania — are usually much cheaper than private loans. Read the repayment rules: when repayments start and what happens if you don’t pay.
Borrow for things that grow your future (fees, a laptop for your course) — not for things that are gone next week.
keyPoints: Borrow for your future, not for fun
quiz: What is the “principal”? | The interest ; The amount you borrowed ; The bank manager | 2 | Principal is the original amount borrowed.
A lender charges 5% a month. The yearly cost is roughly… | 5% ; 60% ; about 80% (with compounding) | 3 | 1.05¹² ≈ 1.80 — about 80% a year.
Which is usually cheapest? | Digital app loans ; Government student loans ; Borrowing from a shopkeeper | 2 | Government student loan schemes are designed to be affordable.

moneyLessons.title: Avoiding debt traps
moneyLessons.summary: Quick app loans, betting and “pay later” offers are built to keep you borrowing.
body: Instant mobile and app loans feel small, but the fees are often charged every week or month. A 10% fee for a 30-day loan works out to over 200% a year.
Borrowing to repay another loan is the clearest sign of a debt trap. Stop, list everything you owe, and talk to someone you trust or the university’s financial aid office.
Betting is designed so the house wins over time. Never bet with fee, rent or food money.
Late payments can be reported to a Credit Reference Bureau (CRB). A bad record can block you from loans and some jobs later.
keyPoints: Check the yearly cost of “small” loans
Never borrow to repay a loan
quiz: A 10% fee on a 30-day loan is roughly how much per year? | 10% ; 120% ; over 200% | 3 | Compounded monthly: 1.10¹² ≈ 3.1 — over 200% a year.
What is a warning sign of a debt trap? | Paying rent on time ; Borrowing to repay another loan ; Saving every month | 2 | Borrowing to repay borrowing means debt is growing.
Where can late payments be recorded? | Nowhere ; A Credit Reference Bureau ; Your student ID | 2 | Credit bureaus keep records lenders check.

moneyLessons.title: Exchange rates and paying fees abroad
moneyLessons.summary: If your fees are in pounds, dollars or euros, the shilling’s value can change your bill.
body: An exchange rate tells you how much of one currency you get for another. Rates move every day.
If your fees are set in another currency and your shilling gets weaker, you pay more shillings for the same fee — even though the university didn’t raise anything.
Banks and money transfer services also take a spread: the rate they give you is worse than the rate you see on the news. Compare the total amount received, not the advertised fee.
Protect yourself with a buffer of 10–15% in your plan, and pay large amounts early when you can.
keyPoints: Foreign fees can rise when your currency falls
Compare the amount received, not just the fee
Pay big amounts early if possible
quiz: Your fee is £10,000. The shilling weakens. What happens in shillings? | It goes down ; It stays the same ; It goes up | 3 | A weaker shilling buys fewer pounds, so you need more shillings.
What’s the best way to compare transfer services? | Lowest advertised fee ; Most money received at the other end ; Nicest website | 2 | The rate spread can cost more than the fee.
A sensible exchange-rate buffer is about… | 0% ; 10–15% ; 100% | 2 | 10–15% covers normal swings for most plans.

moneyLessons.title: Family money and sponsors
moneyLessons.summary: Most students are funded by family. Clear, kind conversations prevent most money crises.
body: Have the money conversation early: show your family the true cost of your course — not just tuition.
Ask for a clear amount and timing in writing (a message is fine). This also helps for visas and sponsor letters.
Keep receipts and share a short update each semester: what was paid and what’s coming next. Trust grows when people can see where money goes.
If the plan changes (a sponsor can’t pay), tell your university’s financial aid office immediately — before fees are overdue.
keyPoints: Agree amounts and dates in writing
Tell the university early if plans change
quiz: When should you discuss the full cost with family? | After the first fees are due ; Before you accept an offer ; Only if asked | 2 | Early conversations prevent surprises.
Why get the agreed amount in writing? | It helps planning, visas and trust ; Banks require it ; It’s a legal contract | 1 | It’s clear, and it doubles as evidence for sponsor letters.
Your sponsor can’t pay next semester. First step? | Hide it ; Tell the financial aid office now ; Take an app loan | 2 | Universities can often offer plans or bursaries if you ask early.

moneyLessons.title: Money scams students face
moneyLessons.summary: Scammers target students with fake scholarships, fake agents and urgent payment requests.
body: Real scholarships don’t charge you to apply or to “release” your award.
Pay university fees only to the accounts printed on your official offer letter or portal — never to a person’s mobile money number.
Be suspicious of urgency (“pay in 2 hours or lose your place”) and secrecy (“don’t tell your parents”).
If you’re unsure, contact the university or scholarship using the details on its official website — not the details in the message.
keyPoints: No fee to apply for real scholarships
quiz: A “scholarship” asks UGX 200,000 to process your award. It’s… | Normal ; A red flag ; A government fee | 2 | Real scholarships don’t charge to release awards.
Where should you pay tuition? | Agent’s mobile money ; Accounts on your official offer/portal ; Any account the caller gives | 2 | Only official accounts.
Best way to check a suspicious message? | Reply to it ; Call the number in the message ; Use contacts on the official website | 3 | Never trust contact details inside a suspicious message.

moneyLessons.title: Your first income: payslips and tax
moneyLessons.summary: Gross pay isn’t what lands in your account. Understand your payslip before you plan your spending.
body: Gross pay is the full salary agreed. Net pay (take-home) is what you receive after deductions.
Common deductions are income tax (PAYE), social security / pension contributions (for example NSSF) and sometimes health insurance or loan repayments.
Always budget with your net pay. When comparing job offers, ask what the take-home will be.
Keep your payslips — you’ll need them for loans, rentals and visas.
quiz: What is net pay? | Salary before deductions ; Take-home after deductions ; Your bonus | 2 | Net = what actually reaches your account.
Which should you budget with? | Gross ; Net ; The highest offer you heard about | 2 | Only money you actually receive can be spent.
PAYE is… | A savings plan ; Income tax taken from your salary ; A bank fee | 2 | Pay As You Earn — income tax deducted by your employer.
